# Deuteronomy 6: research notes

**Gaps to know about first.** Enduringword.com wouldn't load (the tool refused that URL), and the Blue Letter Bible copy of Guzik's study guide came back as menus only, so his comments below are just short search snippets. The Precept Austin page cut off after verse 1. I found nothing from Catholic or Orthodox sites (newadvent, catholic.com, oca.org), Lutheran sites, Pentecostal writers, or on prosperity or hyper-grace teaching about this chapter, so those are left out. Matthew Henry is the only source I read for every verse, which means vv. 10–24 depend mostly on him.

---

**v. 1**
- In the Hebrew, "commandment" is singular. The NET note says this may make it a summary word for the whole law, with "statutes and ordinances" explaining it. The Pulpit Commentary calls it the "sum and substance" of what God commanded. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-6-commentary
- Trapp says Moses now starts explaining the Ten Commandments, beginning with the first. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-6-commentary
- Matthew Henry says Moses taught exactly what God told him to, no more and no less, just as Christ's ministers should (Matt 28:20). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/deuteronomy/6.htm

**v. 2**
- Merrill: teaching the law produces godly fear, fear leads to obedience, and obedience is the condition for long life in the land. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-6-commentary
- Henry: fear of God in the heart is the strongest motive for obedience. Faith passed down to children and grandchildren is the best inheritance. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/deuteronomy/6.htm

**v. 3**
- Henry: faith and righteousness help a people prosper, so "fear God, and it shall be well with thee." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/deuteronomy/6.htm

**v. 4: how to translate it, and the Trinity**
- **Meaning:** Barnes calls these words "the creed of the Jews," recited morning and evening.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/6-4.htm
- **Two possible translations:** The Hebrew can be read "the LORD alone" (Yahweh is the only God for Israel) or "one LORD" (God is a unity). The commentator quoted on StudyLight says the second reading does not conflict with the Trinity. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/6-4.html The NET note favours "the LORD alone," pointing to the calls for loyalty in vv. 5 and 14 and to "one" meaning "one of a kind" in Song 6:8–9. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Deu+6%3A4-5 Precept Austin agrees the main point is that the LORD is unique, with his indivisibility as a secondary point. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-6-commentary
- **Calvin (Reformed):** "one" covers more than God's essence. It also means the power and glory God had shown Israel, so turning from him would be rebellion. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/6-4.html
- **Does it hint at the Trinity?** Commentators split:
  - *Yes, a hint:* Matthew Henry says the name of God appears three times and the word "God" is plural, which seems to point to three persons.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/6-4.htm
  - *Yes, strongly:* Chuck Smith argues that *echad* means a compound unity and that the Trinity is "right there" in the Shema. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/6-4.html
  - *More cautious:* Ellicott says the Trinity can be seen in the Old Testament only by the light of the New, and was not explicitly revealed until Christ came.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/6-4.htm A source quoted by Precept Austin says the verse focuses on there being one God and on Israel's exclusive loyalty. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-6-commentary
  - *Guzik:* Christians need to recover a sense of God's unity, though the verse certainly does not contradict the truth of the Trinity. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/deuteronomy/deuteronomy-6.cfm
- **Ligonier (Reformed):** the first commandment's ban on other gods rests on the Shema. Because God alone is God, no other "deity" may be served at all. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/hear-o-israel
- **Modern scholarship (Bible Odyssey, Shawna Dolansky):** the Hebrew is ambiguous and could mean "YHWH is our god, YHWH alone." That would express *monolatry*: other gods might exist, but Israel must worship only YHWH. She says vv. 12–13 fit this reading. https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/the-shema/

**v. 5**
- **Heart, soul, strength:** Barnes reads the heart as the seat of understanding, the soul as the centre of will and personality, and "might" as all of a person's energies. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/6-5.htm Keil and Delitzsch say "all your heart" rules out half-heartedness, and that this love is the root from which keeping the commandments was meant to grow. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/6-5.htm
- **Should the three words be separated?** Constable quotes a scholar who says the verse does not invite analysis into ideas of intellectual, emotional, and physical parts. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/6-5.html The NET note says "soul" (*nefesh*) in the Old Testament means the whole person, unlike Greek ideas of a separate soul. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Deu+6%3A4-5
- **"Might" (Desiring God, Baptist):** the Hebrew word usually means "very." Following Daniel Block, the article suggests it covers all our resources. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/love-god-with-your-everything Ellicott notes that Rashi read it as "all thy money." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/6-5.htm
- **Matthew Henry:** our love for God should be sincere, strong, above every other love, informed by knowledge, and undivided. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/deuteronomy/6.htm
- **Benson:** a command to love "with all thy heart" shows the Sinai covenant was never merely external. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/6-5.htm
- **New Testament:** Jesus calls this the first and great commandment (Matt 22:37–40). Constable notes that Josiah is the only Old Testament figure said to have turned to the LORD with heart, soul, and might (2 Kgs 23:25). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/6-5.html
- **A distinctive evangelical view (The Bible Says):** the source explains vv. 4–5 using ancient treaties between a great king and a lesser king. It then argues that the commands affect a believer's *fellowship* with God and enjoyment of his blessings, not their relationship to him, which rests on faith alone. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/tbs/meaning/deu-6-v4-5.cfm

**v. 6**
- Henry: laying God's words on the heart (meditation) follows directly from loving God. He that loves God loves his Bible. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/deuteronomy/6.htm

**v. 7**
- Henry notes the alternative reading "whet them," as when sharpening a knife: keep repeating the truths to children from every side. He cites Bishop Patrick's point that the law was plain enough for any parent to teach. He also says all of life's ordinary moments are occasions to talk about God's plain truths. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/deuteronomy/6.htm
- JFB thinks the wording of v. 7, and perhaps v. 8, is probably figurative for constant, earnest teaching. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/6-8.htm

**vv. 8–9: literal or figurative?**
- **Jewish practice:** Ellicott says this verse is the source of the *tefillin* (small scripture boxes worn on the head and arm). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/6-8.htm Coffman says the Jews read these verses literally from the start, producing fringes, tefillin, and the *mezuzah* (a doorpost scroll). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/6-8.html
- **Background:** Barnes and JFB suggest Moses took over Egyptian customs, such as amulets and doorpost inscriptions, and filled them with God's law instead of superstition. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/6-8.htm
- **Henry:** in Moses' day written copies of the law were rare, so these practices helped. Christ blamed the Pharisees for making their phylacteries extra-large, not for wearing them (Matt 23:5). Henry says the command bound Jews in its letter and binds Christians in its intent: keep God's word always to hand. He praises the early English Reformers for painting scripture on church walls when Bibles were scarce. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/deuteronomy/6.htm
- **Bible Odyssey:** however v. 4 is read, the Shema was consistently used for protection (to ward off harm), as these verses show. https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/the-shema/

**vv. 10–12**
- Henry: getting cities and vineyards without effort made the gift richer, but also made it easy to forget the Giver. Prosperity is a dangerous time for forgetting God (Prov 30:9). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/deuteronomy/6.htm

**v. 13**
- Henry: "swear by his name" means appealing to no other god as judge of the truth. It can also mean openly confessing God (Isa 45:23 with Rom 14:11). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/deuteronomy/6.htm
- Barnes: Moses is not encouraging oaths. He is forbidding oaths in any other god's name. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/6-25.html
- Clarke (Methodist): swearing by God's name means treating him as the source of truth and the one who rewards and punishes. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/6-25.html

**vv. 14–15**
- Henry cites Patrick, who cites Maimonides: Scripture speaks of God's anger or jealousy only in connection with idolatry. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/deuteronomy/6.htm

**v. 16**
- Henry: testing God means distrusting his power and care. Jesus quoted this verse against Satan (Matt 4:7). We test God either by despairing of him while we obey, or by presuming on him when we disobey. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/deuteronomy/6.htm

**vv. 17–19**
- Henry: carelessness will ruin us, and we cannot be saved without diligence. Obedience is right in God's eyes and also good for us: "Do well, and it shall be well with thee." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/deuteronomy/6.htm

**vv. 20–23**
- Henry: a child's question about the law is a good sign. Parents should answer that the laws remember the rescue from Egypt. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/deuteronomy/6.htm
- Coffman cites Phillips: this is not a formal "ancient creed," as some scholars claim, but a simple explanation of how Israel got the land. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/6-25.html

**v. 24**
- Henry: God commands only what is truly for our good, so obeying him is in our interest as well as our duty. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/deuteronomy/6.htm

**v. 25: the clearest disagreement between traditions**
- **Gill (Baptist, Calvinist):** this righteousness would require keeping every command perfectly, which no sinner can do. Only Christ could thus keep all the commandments of God, and his obedience is our righteousness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/6-25.htm
- **Geneva Study Bible:** no one can fully obey the law, we must turn to Christ to be justified by faith. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/6-25.htm
- **Matthew Henry:** perfect obedience would justify us, but since we can't manage it, sincere obedience is accepted through a Mediator. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/deuteronomy/6.htm
- **Clarke (Methodist):** the righteousness is evidence that we are under the influence of the fear and love of God. Moses is not saying it can be achieved without God's mercy or that it buys heaven. The goal is holiness of heart and conduct. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/6-25.html
- **Barnes:** God will treat us as righteous, and Moses made the law's righteousness depend on the heart, in one word, upon faith. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/6-25.html
- **Keil and Delitzsch:** this is not the gospel "righteousness of faith," but the two don't conflict, because it rests on wholehearted love that needs living faith. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/6-25.htm
- **Constable** quotes a scholar who says later Judaism wrongly made covenant-keeping the basis of righteousness, when it was meant to express faith. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/6-25.html
- **Reading it as "mercy":** Poole and Benson prefer "mercy shall be to us," because the Hebrew word often means mercy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/6-25.htm The Douay-Rheims, a Catholic translation, likewise reads "he will be merciful to us." https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/brl/deuteronomy/6-25.html
- **Ancient translations:** Ellicott notes the Targum reads "merit" and the Greek Septuagint "alms," which explains why Matt 6:1 has "alms" in some versions and "righteousness" in others. The Cambridge Bible takes the word as vindication or the right to live. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/6-25.htm
